title: Amrit when you're ready
hook: five stood up in 1699, each by his own choice; amrit waits for your yes
carry: amrit waits for your own yes
tomorrow: Simran gets her first job. what makes money clean?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a father who ran while his son was yet a great way off, and a sangat with no check at the door: not yet is fine. Tonight the whole family is at dinner.

Every family dinner has one relative who asks the question everyone else was too polite to ask. In Simran's family it's Chacha Ji, her dad's younger brother, between the dal and the rice: so, Simran, when's your amrit? Jasleen took it, no? The table goes quiet. Harjit stares at his plate. Bebe Jaswant puts down her spoon.
screen: `THE QUESTION NOBODY ELSE ASKS.` → `SO, WHEN'S YOUR AMRIT?` → `BEBE PUTS DOWN HER SPOON.`

segments.voice: Bebe's answer is short. Some take it young. Some take it with gray hair. I took it after you were born, she tells Chacha Ji, and nobody hurried me. Then she tells the story every Sikh child knows. Vaisakhi, 1699, at Anandpur. A great crowd has gathered. Guru Gobind Singh comes out with a sword and asks: who will give his head? Silence. Then one man stands. The Guru asks again, and again, until five have stood. Each one rose on his own; nobody was pulled from his seat. Those five became the Panj Pyare, the five beloved, the first to receive amrit, and to this day five Sikhs give it. That's the teaching under the dinner question: amrit is a lifelong commitment, so it has to be your own yes. The Sikh code sets no age; it asks that a person be willing and old enough to understand. Look back over the week: the head already on the palm, the daily banis and five Ks, the five who give, a new beginning, and not yet is fine. They all say one thing to Chacha Ji: the pace belongs to the person. Simran says it herself, smiling: I'm thinking about it. When I'm ready, you'll be the first to know. Chacha Ji laughs and asks for more rice.
screen: `VAISAKHI 1699: WHO WILL GIVE HIS HEAD?` · `FIVE STOOD UP, EACH ON HIS OWN.` · `NO AGE IN THE CODE.` · `THE PACE BELONGS TO THE PERSON.` · then, large: `EVERYONE'S PACE.`

segments.voice: If you pray, sit and repeat Waheguru quietly, the simran Sikhs do every day, at whatever pace your breath sets. Don't hurry it and don't drag it. If you don't pray, sit with one slow sound around you, a fan or your own breathing, and let it keep its own speed.
Everyone's pace. No pressure toward amrit, and no judging how fast or slow anyone comes to it.
Your line: amrit waits for your own yes. Five stood up in 1699, each by himself, and Simran's pace belongs to Simran. That's the week.

howItsDone: Sikh families and gurdwaras encourage amrit, and the step itself is left to the person, taken when they are ready.

banis.meaning: set hymns of the Gurus recited daily

Panj Pyare.meaning: the five beloved: the five who stood up in 1699 and first received amrit
